author: Carlos Martinez
title: Aston Martin Vantage GT4 iRacing Setup and Driving Guide
description: Master the Vantage GT4's balance of power and agility. Learn setup tuning, brake technique, and racecraft for consistent GT4 wins on iRacing.

sections.p: The Aston Martin Vantage GT4 is one of my favorite cars to race on iRacing. It's not the quickest car in the GT4 lineup, but it rewards smooth inputs and precision far more than raw aggression. I've found that once you dial in the balance and respect the tire envelope, the Vantage is genuinely competitive across both road courses and street circuits. The car teaches you discipline—something that translates directly to faster lap times and cleaner races.

I'll walk you through my baseline setup philosophy, the brake calibration that works best on my MOZA CRP2 pedals, and the driving techniques that let me stay consistent over a stint. The Vantage isn't forgiving if you're sloppy, but that's exactly why it's so rewarding to master.

The Vantage GT4 sits in the middle of the GT4 field in terms of top-end speed, but it generates excellent mid-corner grip when the setup is balanced. I start with anti-roll bars (ARBs) that aren't too stiff—around 8–10 front, 12–14 rear on most road courses. Too much rear stiffness will understeer the car and kill your corner exit speed; too little will make it unpredictable under braking and in tight turns.

Brake balance is critical. I typically run around 52–54% rear bias on road courses. The front end of the Vantage is responsive, so it's easy to lock the fronts if you're over-braking. That 52–54% window keeps the car balanced under heavy braking without inducing premature rear locking.

list: Anti-roll bars: 8–10 front, 12–14 rear (adjust +/- 2 if understeering or oversteering consistently)
Brake balance: 52–54% rear (higher on tracks with long straights; lower on tight circuits)
Differential lock: 40–45% acceleration, 45–50% deceleration (more lock helps exit traction)
Ride height: ~40–45mm front, ~50–55mm rear (lower is faster, but watch for bottoming on bumpy tracks)
Camber: -2.5° to -3.0° front, -1.5° to -2.0° rear (track surface and tire degradation matter)

sections.tip: The Vantage's V12 makes ~600 hp—enough to overstep the rear tires if you're careless on corner exit. Dial in progressively. If you're spinning out mid-corner or at the exit, reduce rear ARB by 1–2 points before adding throttle map.

sections.p: I've noticed the Vantage GT4 runs relatively cool tires compared to the more aggressive GT4 cars (like the BMW M4 GT4). Your tire pressures tend to stay steady across a stint, which is a blessing—it means your setup doesn't drift as much as the stint progresses. I start with pressures around 27.0–27.5 psi front, 27.5–28.0 psi rear, and they usually climb to 27.8–28.5 psi by lap 10–12 of steady racing.

The real challenge is tire life. The Vantage isn't as kind to the rears as some GT4 cars. If you're defending a position or pushing hard through the middle of a race, you'll feel the rear tires starting to fade after 35–40 minutes of heavy use. This means you need a strategy: either manage your pace through the middle stints and attack late, or qualify well enough that you're not defending.

list: Tire pressures: Start 27.0–27.5 F, 27.5–28.0 R; monitor climb to avoid overheating
Rear tire life: Plan for noticeable grip loss after 35–40 minutes of sustained pace
Temperature: Keep tire temps in the 85–95°C range; hotter and wear accelerates, cooler and the tires won't grip
Qualification strategy: A clean, committed qualifying lap is worth more than a desperate mid-race recovery

sections.p: My MOZA CRP2 load-cell pedals give me excellent feel, and that's essential with the Vantage. The car responds sharply to brake input—there's little margin for sloppy pedal work. I brake earlier than I might in an easier car, but carry brake pressure deeper into corners through trail braking.

On my pedals, I apply ~75–80% brake pressure initially (firm enough to load the fronts without locking), then trail down to 20–40% as I rotate into the apex. The load cell gives me precise feedback—I can feel when I'm at the edge of grip and dial the pressure back fractionally if needed. This technique is where the Vantage shines: it rewards smooth, progressive inputs.

For corner sequences (like the infield at Watkins Glen or the carousel at Daytona Road Course), I often carry 15–20% throttle overlap—trailing brakes and beginning throttle application simultaneously. This keeps the car stable and planted while building speed out of the corner.

olist: Identify your braking point (typically 50–75 meters before the corner depending on the track)
Apply firm initial brake pressure (~75–80%) to load the front tires
Trail brake progressively as you approach the apex, reducing pressure to 20–40%
Begin throttle application smoothly as you unwind the steering wheel; overlap brake and throttle by 1–2 tenths
Exit with consistent throttle application—don't stab the accelerator

sections.h2: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

sections.p: The Vantage GT4 forgives impatience more than it forgives sloppiness. Most of my mistakes in this car come from one of these habits:

list: Over-braking under frustration: I'll see a gap and stab the brake, locking the fronts and plowing into a corner. Respect the brake pedal; smooth inputs are always faster.
Rushing the throttle exit: The V12 will step the rear out if you floor it too early. Build throttle progressively through the exit; patience gains tenths.

Carrying too much speed into high-speed corners: The Vantage can understeer badly if you're carrying too much entry speed. Brake a tick earlier; you'll carry more mid-corner speed and a higher exit velocity.
Ignoring tire temperature: If your tire temps are consistently above 95°C or below 80°C, your brake balance or ARBs are off. Tweak and retest.
Not adjusting for fuel load: A full tank makes the Vantage significantly slower and less responsive. Compensate by braking earlier and being smoother on throttle in the first few laps.

sections.tip: On first lap after a pit stop (with fresh fuel), I immediately dial back my aggression by 10–15%. The car feels slower because it is. By lap 3–4 of the stint, fuel burn has improved confidence and lap times.

sections.p: The Vantage GT4 performs well on circuits with flowing corners and long straights, but struggles slightly at tracks with tight, technical corners (like Brands Hatch or Oulton Park). I adjust my strategy based on the venue:

list: Road America, Watkins Glen, COTA: Increase rear ARB by 1–2 points to sharpen turn-in; the Vantage needs help rotating in fast corners.
Sebring, Laguna Seca: Reduce ride height slightly for better mechanical grip over bumps; the Vantage is stiff-natured and doesn't love undulation.
Daytona Road Course, Sonoma: Keep baseline setup; these suits the Vantage's power delivery and smooth mid-corner grip.
Brands Hatch, Oulton Park: Add soft-spring setup and reduce anti-roll bars to improve turn-in feel; the tight corners need sharper initial response.

sections.p: In a race, the Vantage GT4 is a defensive car. Its strength is consistency and mid-corner grip, not raw pace. I focus on driving clean lines, hitting my marks, and keeping my tire temps in the sweet zone. Defending relies on discipline: I don't move unnecessarily under braking, I don't overcomplicate lines, and I don't pick fights I can't win.

On the straights, the Vantage is middle-of-the-pack. You're not going to out-drag a BMW M4 GT4 or a Porsche 911 GT4, so don't try. Instead, brake later, turn in sharper, and exit tighter than the car behind you. Make the corner so good that by the time you're accelerating, you've already built an advantage.

In traffic or multi-class racing, the Vantage's responsive steering is an asset. I can weave through slower cars with confidence and make quick directional changes. Respect their racing line, give space in the braking zones, and your precision will carry you past them naturally.

The Aston Martin Vantage GT4 has become my go-to car for grinding iRacing GT4 races because it doesn't reward cutting corners—literally or figuratively. It demands respect, but once you dial in the setup and commit to smooth technique, lap times come down and confidence rises. I've won races in the Vantage not because it's the quickest car, but because I've been precise enough to keep tires and brake temps optimal while competitors ahead of me have either overdone it or managed their resources poorly. That's racing, and the Vantage teaches it well.

faqs.q: What is the best brake balance for the Aston Martin Vantage GT4 on iRacing?
faqs.a: I run 52–54% rear bias on most road courses. The exact setting depends on track layout—longer braking zones may benefit from 54–55%, while tight circuits work better at 50–52%. Start at 52% and adjust by 1% increments if you're locking fronts consistently (increase bias) or locking rears (decrease bias). Test in practice and adjust during the race if needed.

faqs.q: How do I prevent the Vantage GT4 from understeering in mid-corner?
faqs.a: Understeer in the Vantage typically means your rear anti-roll bar is too stiff or your brake trail is too aggressive. First, reduce rear ARB by 1–2 points and test. If that doesn't help, try braking 1–2 meters earlier and carrying less speed into the corner—the Vantage rewards precision entry over raw entry speed. Tire temperature also matters: cool tires (below 85°C) will understeer more than hot tires.

faqs.q: What is the Vantage GT4's ideal tire pressure range?
faqs.a: I start at 27.0–27.5 psi front and 27.5–28.0 psi rear. Pressures climb during the race; monitor them around lap 10 and adjust if they exceed 28.5 psi front or 29.0 psi rear. If pressures are rising too fast, your brake balance may be too aggressive or your ride height too low. Slightly reduce brake pressure overlap or raise the car by 2–3 mm and retest.

faqs.q: How long can I push the Vantage GT4 hard before tire wear becomes a factor?
faqs.a: Plan on 35–40 minutes of sustained, aggressive pace before rear tire grip drops noticeably. In a 1-hour race, I push hard for the first 30 minutes, manage pace in the middle 20 minutes, then push again in the final 10 if I'm in contention. If you're qualifying or defending a podium position, expect to feel tire fatigue by lap 30–35 of constant high-effort driving.
